articles.title: Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings . “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”
Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.
For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.
The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.
The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.
But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported .

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro , the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.
Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.
“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.
Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June . Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands , AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B , is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog . “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”
Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported .

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.
Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported . An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.
AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.
If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

articles.title: Don’t miss Seattle tech’s biggest holiday party: Get early bird tickets for the GeekWire Gala

articles.title: Tech Moves: Microsoft loses a CVP to AWS and gains one from Alteryx; Lila Bio and BECU name execs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — After more than 33 years at Microsoft, Mazhar Mohammed has left to become vice president of AWS Streaming and Messaging at Amazon .

Mohammed joined Microsoft as a software design engineer on Windows NT straight out of a master’s degree program. Over the decades, he also worked on messaging, mobile services and partner experience for cloud services. He most recently served as corporate VP for the commerce and fraud protection platform.
His LinkedIn post was short and to the point. Mohammed said he was “happy to share” the news, and the post featured a photo of an Amazon box with the message “Alexa, play ‘New Beginnings.’”
— Microsoft has named Chad Thompson as CVP of Agent Cloud, a group within the company developing technology that allows businesses to deploy AI agents and put them to work across their organizations.

“My view: enterprise is where AI pays off. Not in demos, but in measurable results. Lower costs, faster cycle times, better decisions, and work that gets done without someone pushing it along,” Thompson wrote in a LinkedIn post.
Thompson joins from Alteryx. He previously spent six years at Amazon, departing as general manager of Amazon Glow. Other past employers include Smartsheet, Exasol and Adobe.

— Gail Carpenter has been named as VP and chief financial officer of Global Entertainment and Advertising at Amazon . She was most recently CFO of Worldwide Stores Finance and has been with the company for 11 years.

— Seattle biotech startup L i la Bio has appointed Kimberly Ma as chief development officer. The company spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington and is using AI to design new proteins that can treat cancer with targeted radiation therapy. Last year it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop therapies for solid tumors.

Ma has 20 years of experience in oncology drug development, most recently as a leader at Abdera Therapeutics. She also worked at RayzeBio, where she led the clinical operations team and supported the company’s IPO and its $4.1 billion acquisition by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024.
— The not-for-profit credit union BECU has named Geoffrey Fonga as VP of AI transformation. The member-owned organization is based in Tukwila, Wash.
“For years, I helped organizations adopt and scale AI as an advisor and a vendor,” Fonga said . “Now I get to do the harder, more rewarding part: leading that transformation from the inside.”
Fonga joins from DataRobot. He previously held leadership roles at McKinsey & Company and Wells Fargo.

— Andre Woodson Jr. has taken a new role at Amazon as manager of U.S. state and local policy communications and external affairs. Woodson was previously a regional field communications manager and has been with the company for more than 12 years.

— Hanna Grene has left Microsoft, where she served as global go-to-market and innovation leader for energy, to join Xcel Energy . She will lead the company’s newly established Enterprise Growth and Commercialization group, effective Nov. 16.
— Seattle-based RevealDx ,which is developing AI technology for detecting potentially cancerous lung nodules, has made two leadership appointments:

— Enterprise software company LogicGate has named two new leaders to the business, which is headquartered in Chicago and has multiple C-suite executives based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. Steve Smith has joined as managing director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Amanda Meglemre as general counsel.

— Former Cisco and Microsoft security executive Edna Conway was appointed to the advisory council for Known , a Bellevue, Wash.-based tech company building accountability infrastructure for AI agents. Conway was with Cisco for 20 years before joining Microsoft in 2020 as VP and chief security and risk officer for Azure infrastructure.

— Avalanche Energy , a Seattle-based startup building fusion devices, has named Chris Riegel as head of talent acquisition. He joins from HiringKit, an HR company that Riegel co-founded. Former employers include Amazon and Unity Technologies.

In addition to chasing fusion, Avalanche is leading a team tackling DARPA’s nuclear battery challenge and launching FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies in Eastern Washington.
— Julie Averill , former chief information officer at lululemon and REI, has joined the UW Foundation Board , which helps raise philanthropic support for the university.
— Technology Alliance has appointed Jen Oleson , a senior director at Seattle-based consulting firm Slalom, to its board. Oleson will serve on the organization’s Research Capacity Committee.
— Ben Helsel has left Premera Blue Cross to join Kaiser Permanente , where he’ll serve as VP and general manager of commercial markets in Washington.

articles.title: Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating
articles.author: Joe Nguyễn
paras: Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email tips@geekwire.com .
How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.
That growing resignation took us to San Francisco . We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.
I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.
And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.
Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.
Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.
Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.
San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.
People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.
Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.
San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.
Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.
Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.
What might we accomplish if we recovered it?
Read the full series, starting with Part 1 .

articles.title: Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.
The change, announced Monday , opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.
For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.
Microsoft Foundry , the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.
The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.
Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000 .

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules . To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.
The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

articles.title: Sara Nelson Leads Dark Money Attacks on Jenks, Seeking to Keep Centrists' Grip on Seattle Council
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: As Election Day arrives, much holds in the balance. Nationally, attention will be on whether polling that hints at a national blue wave will allow Democrats to seize control of both chambers of Congress will come to pass and provide a check on President Donald Trump's power and erratic decision making.

Locally, a special election in Seattle Council District 5 presents an opportunity for the progressive coalition to gain a seat and momentum heading into the 2027 election when all seven district seats will be on the ballot. Progressive standard-bearer Nilu Jenks has the advantage based on primary results , when she won 54% of the vote. The Urbanist Elections Committee (on which I serve) endorsed Jenks .
However, centrist donors are spending aggressively to prop up former bank chair Julie Kang in hopes of closing the gap. They're using a familiar formula , seeking to paint Jenks as soft on crime.

In their haste, a pro-Kang political action committee (PAC) called North Seattle Neighbors potentially broke election laws to rush attack ads out the door, and the Jenks campaign is calling on the PAC to fully disclose its donors and has appealed to the Seattle Ethics and Elections Commission seeking a cease-and-desist order barring it from "any further political advertising until it files every overdue report and discloses all its contributors and the true sources of its money."
John Wyble, a spokesperson for the Jenks campaign, argued this dark money-fueled attack ads has no place in Seattle politics.

"This is how Republican super PACs operate in swing states: scary pictures, old quotes, and money nobody can trace. It has no place in a Seattle council race," Wyble said. "The PAC can't keep its own donor list straight, and the people who put up most of the money won't say who they are. District 5 voters deserve to know who's paying to fill their mailboxes, and they deserve to know before they vote."

Interestingly, a major funnel of this dark money was Seattle's former Council president who lost her seat in a 2025 election drubbing: "SeaFor is a 501(c)(4) formed by former Councilmember Sara Nelson. It is not registered with the PDC or SEEC and does not disclose its donors," the Jenks campaign noted. "According to PubliCola, its website pitched the structure as protecting 'the privacy of businesses and individuals.'"

After the Jenks campaign filed its complaint and publications like PubliCola reported on it , the pro-Kang PAC said it returned the $30,000 donation from Nelson's SeaFor group. The PAC already spent the money on mailers so returning the check that accounted for two thirds of its fundraising has sunk it into debt, forcing it to ramp up fundraising – potentially to the same donors using SeaFor.

Without the SeaFor smoke screen to hide behind, the donors will eventually be revealed, although likely not until after ballot boxes close. The contributors that North Seattle Neighbors does list include former interim Seattle Mayor Tim Burgess and several real estate bigshots including Vulcan's chief real estate officer Ada Healey, Fremont land baron Suzie Burke, and Judith Runstad.

Nelson has indicated that SeaFor's 2026 spends are a test run on a broader 2027 strategy to keep control of Seattle Council in centrist hands – currently Council's progressive wing has just three members, while six councilmembers are some shade of centrist.

The other major endeavor SeaFor is engaged in: running a website built on AI-slop city hall "reporting." The website appears geared toward galvanizing more conservative leaning folks to submit comments to Council.

It remains to be seen whether Nelson and her friends will need to pull off a D5 comeback to provide a proof of concept to megadonors on their dark money project, or whether simply keeping it fairly close will be proof enough. The 2027 council elections are likely to involve big spending, either way, if recent elections are any indication.

Political cartoonist and comedian Brett Hamil argued letting Nelson get away with this scheme would set a dangerous precedent: “Sara Nelson, Tanya Woo & the Julie Kang PAC (“North Seattle Neighbors”) are in the midst of the biggest campaign finance scandal possibly ever in Seattle, and if they face no serious consequences they will run the same playbook for seven city council seats next year.”

The PAC attacks have focused on Jenks' opposition to expanding CCTV camera surveillance and stay out orders for prostitution and public drug use, which she says is based on evidence that those approaches are not effective. Jenks has portrayed public safety as a top priority , but she has emphasized expanding the role of the civilian-run Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) department to boost safety. The question remains of whether surveillance cameras, stay out orders, and some vague police defunding insinuations are salient enough issues to swing voters, or whether voters view public safety from a broader and more nuanced perspective.

For now, most centrist councilmembers appear intent on kneecapping a good chunk of Mayor Katie Wilson's agenda and taking opportunistic political swings at her. Speculation is swirling at city hall that several councilmembers are mulling runs against the mayor when her seat is up in 2029. District-based members would need to survive 2027 reelection bids first unless they want to try pulling a Bruce Harrell and taking two years off from elected office before rebranding as an outsider.
Would the entry of Nilu Jenks shake up this dynamic or simply have centrist doubling down?
Bus funding increases are also on the ballot in Seattle and in Pierce County.

If voters approve it, the Seattle Transit Measure will renew existing bus service support and provide an additional 95,000 bus trips per year to boost service frequency on at least 10 routes . The measure also supports reduced fare programs for low-income residents.

Pierce County's measure , meanwhile, would be an even larger jump in bus investment, boosting Pierce Transit service by 47%. This would put Pierce County in closer parity with its neighbors after more than a decade of failing to approve a transit measure.

The Seattle measure appears likely to pass given the margins recent tax measures have run up in the Emerald City – and passage could give Mayor Katie Wilson some additional momentum building on her recent success speeding up Route 8 for bus riders.

Good news gaining another progressive ally on council and passing a major transit measure could act as a bit of a reset for the mayor – with some local media outlets still fixated on her handling of the fatal Bite of Seattle shooting, even more than three months after the fact.

If progressive seize control of Council in 2027, much larger policy swings would be on the table for Seattle's first progressive mayor in more than a decade. The first step is winning the opening skirmish in 2026.

articles.title: ‘Terima kasih’ — Kedai Makan’s long Capitol Hill journey coming to an end at 15th and Pine — for now
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Kedai Makan’s long, flavorful path across Capitol Hill may not be ending but its days atop the Hill at 15th and Pine are coming to an end.
The Malaysian restaurant that started 15 years ago as a stand at the Broadway farmers market announced its final day of service at its current Capitol Hill location is coming later this month:

Our Capitol Hill lease is coming to an end, and Sunday, November 15 will be our last day of service there. To everyone who shared a meal, a celebration, or a quiet weeknight with us — terima kasih. You made this neighborhood feel like home.
In the announcement, ownership said they are “exploring the possibility of staying in Capitol Hill” at a new location and that the Kedai Makan location in Belltown will remain open.
Farther Capitol Hill wandering for Kedai Makan would be part of its long story.

The restaurant reopened at 15th and Pine in 2023 under new owners after founders Kevin Burzell and Alysson Wilson decided they were ready to step away. The couple had grown the Malaysian favorite on Bellevue Ave as part of its decade-long path from the Capitol Hill farmers market to years of brick and mortar service along E Olive Way.

Veteran restaurateurs Khampaeng “KP” Panyathong with Joe and Lucy Ye ditched the Money Frog concept they were collaborating on and took over Kedai Makan to move it into the 15th and Pine space. According to city permits, the Ye team has been the sole ownership since 2025.
Kedai Makan’s first brick and mortar location was a counter space along E Olive Way (Image: CHS)

Before the short-lived Money Frog and Kedai Makan’s three-year run in the space, the corner was home to Shota Nakajima’s debut foray on Capitol Hill, the upscale Naka which eventually became Adana . Before Nakajima, French gastropub Le Zinc held down the corner.

The area is home to a cluster of food and drink where 15th meets Pike/Pine including Plenty of Clouds , Travis Post and Lisa Zack’s Sichuan concept that opened in 2018 at the corner, and Brandon Barnato’s pizza and salumi rich Bar Cotto .

articles.title: Override? Council weighs next steps after Wilson veto of RV homeless parking permit plan
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson has drawn a line at City Hall , vetoing a key component of Seattle City Council legislation meant to address RV and trailer homelessness in the city by creating a new parking permit system.

“As mayor, it is my responsibility to ensure that city policies and programs are implementable, a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson wrote in her veto letter (PDF) to the City Clerk .
The legislation’s sponsor Dan Strauss now has up to 30 days to rally an override vote.

In place of the permit program, Wilson is advancing an alternative executive order focused on immediate service deployment rather than administrative permitting. The order directs city departments to immediately release 2026 outreach funding, fast-track the opening and occupancy of two RV safe lots designed to accommodate 182 residents, and establish a cross-departmental and community working group to troubleshoot right-of-way conditions and address neighborhood impacts using existing laws.

The moves challenge the 6–3 majority that passed the RV bill last month. Backing the measure alongside sponsorStrauss (District 6) were Rob Saka (District 1), Maritza Rivera (District 4), Debora Juarez (District 5), Bob Kettle (District 7), and Council President Joy Hollingsworth representing Capitol Hill and the Central District in District 3.
Opposing the plan were councilmembers Dionne Foster, Eddie Lin, and Alexis Mercedes Rinck .

Under the current makeup of the council, Hollingsworth’s centrist-leaning votes are often key in securing a bill’s passage. Representing District 3, Hollingsworth frequently balances neighborhood and small-business concerns over street disorder with practical pathways into shelter and services.
Hollingsworth, who typically takes to her social media accounts to make announcements or statements, has not yet spoken publicly about the RV legislation and the veto.

Meanwhile, the council’s makeup could be shifting. Tuesday’s election will bring a new leader for District 5 where progressive advocate Nilu Jenks and educator Julie Kang are facing off to take the North Seattle council seat vacated by Cathy Moore and currently filled by council veteran Juarez. The winner can take office as soon as the county certifies results which could come within the 30-day window.

As previously reported by CHS , the council designed the Vehicle Resident Assistance Program package to limit long-term vehicular encampments while expanding access to services and shelter. Under the vetoed bill, vehicle residents would have received permits to park in certain zones of the city provided they accepted supportive services.

Wilson, in her letter on the veto, warned against “practical enforcement issues related to towing vehicles that are occupied and increased reliance on SPD to implement a program that has high likelihood of legal liability and personal injury.”
Under the City Charter, council members have up to 30 days to decide to attempt an override. Six votes are needed to counter the mayor’s veto.
The veto is the first of Wilson’s tenure.

articles.title: Meta Keeps Suspending Seattle Bars and Clubs from Instagram
articles.author: Jas Keimig
paras: Massive club owners Kevin Kauer and Ethan Cory were in the middle of doing a supply run for a party on October 22 when Cory received a concerning text from their social media manager. Instagram had suspended the gay club’s account–which boasts around 22,500 followers—without much explanation.

According to Kauer and Cory, the so-called “final straw” for Meta—the Mark Zuckerberg–headed company that owns Instagram—appeared to be Massive’s promotion of Pack Party, a monthly party for Seattle transmascs. The club co-owners said Meta’s AI detection flagged the posts for “conditioning harm” to other people and took down all accounts involved: Massive, Pack Party, and the account belonging to bar manager and Pack Party organizer Max Currie. No one received any further details on what happened and why.

“All they told us was two words: ‘conditioning harm.’ That’s it,” says Cory. “The issue with Meta is that you don’t clearly understand what the rules are. So, if we were to do anything wrong—and nothing we’re doing is wrong—there’s no way to actually amend your actions without going through their AI review.”

The suspension and deletion of Massive, Pack Party, and Currie’s accounts are part of a concerning pattern of gay clubs and promoters across the country being targeted by Meta’s AI detection system. Meta could not be reached for comment on Massive’s Instagram suspension.

Gay clubs exist as spaces for queer people to dance, sip a drink, and meet up with other people in their community, things everyone has a right to do. For a club like Massive, not having access to a platform where they can promote their parties and events to followers means smaller turnouts, directly affecting their bottom line in a business where margins are already small. The suspension of their Instagram last month forced Massive to cancel Bronze Babez, a drag-pole-burlesque show featuring Black and Brown performers.

“We can’t get promotion out, and it means that a whole group of people are now out of a paycheck as well,” says Cory. “It affects more than just our engagement and selling tickets. It means losing a space for a lot of people to just be themselves, for one, and also make money and survive in Seattle, which is obviously a very insanely expensive city.”

Kauer and Cory immediately took to their personal Instagrams , alerting the community about the accounts’ suspension, urging any queers who had an inside track at Meta to help them with the situation. In the past, according to Kauer (who has worked in queer nightlife for two decades), public pressure was the surest way to get accounts back. But as Meta increasingly relies on automated technology to monitor their platforms, it makes it seemingly impossible for suspended accounts to make their case to an actual human without a sympathetic party on the inside.

“You’re not really given the option to ever get justice on it unless you make some huge deal of it, which is super unfair, particularly if a person that’s being affected doesn’t have some large community or business or people behind them to help them out,” says Kauer. “You’re just kind of screwed.”

A few days of back-channeling later, Massive’s Instagram account was restored, only for Massive’s Stripe account—which processes credit card payments on the club’s ticketing site—to then be taken down. The company flagged Massive event descriptions containing the terms “slutty bingo” and “pole dancers.” As they worked with their ticketing company, Tixr, to get their Stripe account back up and running ahead of Massive’s packed Halloweekend event schedule, their Instagram was taken down— again.

“Obviously a human reviewed our things and got [Massive’s Instagram] back. Was it then automatically reported again by the automations? Or did some other human come in and say, ‘No, that’s not OK?’” says Kauer. “We follow the rules the best we can.”

A similar sense of frustration overcame Max Currie, who started the monthly Pack Party at Massive in April 2025 as a way for people under the transmasc umbrella to meet one another, make friends, dance, and find partners in love.

Meta labeling his party as “conditioning harm” is completely against the party’s ethos. “If anything, it’s the opposite,” says Currie. “These events are oftentimes how we can help stop harm in our community, just having a place to go and be around other people who have shared life experiences.” He immediately appealed Meta’s ruling and, three days later, discovered both his personal and Pack Party accounts had been fully deleted. Though Currie still plans on hosting the party every second Thursday at Massive, there’s no clear path forward.

“I’m at a standstill,” he says. “How do I even reach my community without being able to be on social media? How do I promote this event, how do I talk to people about their experiences at the party? It’s been pretty rough.”

This patterned targeting of queer clubs, bars, and promoters isn’t new. According to a Facebook post , CC’s Seattle had their Instagram account suspended in April and denied their appeal for reinstatement. When a bar worker continued to promote CC’s events, their account got suspended as well. As a result, CC’s has been forced to move off of Instagram and mainly posts updates on Bluesky and their website.

Nationally, Meta suspended the Instagram account of historic San Francisco gay bar the Stud in July, falsely flagging it for “engaging in human trafficking.” Only after intense pressure from the public and state senators did the Stud get its account back. In the last year, similar Meta suspensions have hit trans-focused club night Transfix and clubs Catch One, Club Chico, and Club Tempo in Los Angeles, gay bar Rain on 4th in Austin, and Latino gay clubs Next Level and Que Rico in Oakland.

It’s a tricky balancing act for gay bars and promoters. They have to navigate the ever-shifting sensibilities of a large social media platform that is seemingly hostile to their existence, while running a business based on attention. Kauer and Cory say they have had to be extra judicious about what they post on Massive’s Instagram page, nixing party pictures that might have an errant exposed torso or using codes for words like “trans” or “queer” that could set off Meta’s detection system.

“For us to advertise and put our business out in queer nightlife… and make it through the Instagram barriers is a real huge effort,” says Kauer. “And they keep taking you down, or people can report you. It just makes it quite a hellscape, to be honest.”

While Massive got their Stripe account back up before Halloween, their Instagram account is still suspended. The account’s suspension is making Kauer and Cory rethink the club’s entire marketing strategy and consider moving things like ticketing and promoting offline entirely. Currently, the best way to find out about goings-on at Massive is to subscribe to their weekly email newsletter. Though they currently have 15,000 subscribers, Kauer says the email “open” rate sits at around 8 percent.

For better or worse, social media platforms like Instagram are the de facto way to get word out about parties, DJ nights, and drag shows they host each week. Not having it hurts attendance, which, in turn, affects their ability to keep the bar above water. But being on a platform like Instagram or Facebook puts gay bars like theirs in a position that’s beholden to the whims of Meta’s technology.

“Massive is like many businesses that, unfortunately, rely heavily on Instagram. We’ve worked really hard this whole time to build it naturally and to make it fun and engaging and work for our club while still following their rules,” says Kauer. “Then to take it away, I mean, they’re just dinging a small business that’s already fighting to survive.”

articles.title: Katie Wilson Vetoes Strauss’ RV Ban
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson issued her first veto yesterday against a specialized permitting scheme that would effectively ban most homeless RV residents from living in the city.

Sponsored by City Councilmember Dan Strauss, the bill would require people living in RVs and other large vehicles to go through arduous paperwork to retain the right to park for 72 hours on city streets. Only people surveyed in a one-time census would be eligible for that permit, and they could lose it if they refuse offers of shelter too many times. It passed two weeks ago by a vote of 6 to 3.

In a letter to the council, Wilson said the permit program would be difficult to enforce, administratively complicated, expose the City to potential lawsuits, and potentially lead to more people becoming unsheltered.

The mayor did sign Strauss’ four other ordinances that will authorize the City to establish new large vehicle storage lots, boost funding for outreach workers, and redefine the definition of “junk vehicles.”

Initially, it looked like Wilson would allow the RV ban to stand, given that it was passed with a veto-proof majority. However, heavy pressure from homelessness advocates and some of her progressive allies seems to have changed her mind. Alison Eisinger, the executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, says Wilson needed to draw a line in the sand against the morally wrong and ineffective ban.

“I think it’s reasonable to hope that some of those council members will recognize this policy was not ready for prime time,” Eisinger said. “It was not likely to actually resolve homelessness among people who live in RVs, and we can do better.”
In a press release , Strauss showed how bummed he was that Wilson changed her mind, saying “the mayor gave me a call at 4 p.m. to let me know she was breaking that promise [to not veto it].”

The legislation has highlighted the clear fracture between the council’s three progressive members and its centrist majority that was mostly elected in the 2023 backlash election. In order to avoid being overridden, Wilson will need to peel off one of those moderates.

Progressive City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, who urged Wilson to issue the veto, plans to join her at a press conference later today. In a text message to The Stranger , she said the policy would be “cruel,” “impossible for the city to implement,” and “leave hundreds of people without shelter.”
According to Eisinger, almost 600 constituents sent emails to the council and Wilson in opposition to the RV ban. The council has up to 30 days to decide on whether to override the veto.

articles.title: Carrie at 50: Brian De Palma’s fiery masterpiece still has the power

Often when a pop culture figure, whether real or fictional or somewhere in between, is described as an eternal teenager, it refers to an image of youthful vitality. Carrie White, the wallflowery, telekinetic, sort-of heroine at the center of Stephen King’s book and its multiple adaptations, is a sadder case. She’s forever a teenager because until recently, every version of the story ends with her demise – a turn that would qualify as a spoiler if not for the universal familiarity of her story, or the fact that the book heavily implies her fate within the first 30 pages or so.

That fate is poised to change with Mike Flanagan’s TV series , which was recently renewed for a second season (though even then, there’s still plenty of room for poor Carrie to die young). The new show updates and expands the story of the 1974 novel, taking its inspiration from a combination of 2020s social trends and details from the original text. In other words, it’s a new adaptation, not a remake of the Brian De Palma film from 1976. As such, it’s the first truly successful version of Carrie in half a century. (Previous iterations popped up in a 1999 movie sequel, a 2002 miniseries and another film in 2013 .) It’s arguable, however, that the reason such a high-profile new version of Carrie exists in 2026 is that first film, which was released 50 years ago on 3 November.

articles.title: Meta’s $25B fine left out accountability for harm from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal
articles.author:
<name>Emma L. Briant, Visiting Associate Professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data and Society, University of Notre Dame</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/emma-l-briant-146653"/>
paras: “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The US$25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election.

But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica – not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting .

I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare . My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistelblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations . I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely.

My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data.
The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse.

The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.”

The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data.

At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E.U., not events in the U.S.

A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “ People You May Know ,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse . Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica.
Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated.

In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states.

The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.
A decade-old matter - Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal - was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.

From the 2019 Federal Trade Commission order to the 2022 class action settlement to August 2026’s multistate deal , settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime.

Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the lack of comprehensive U.S. privacy legislation , but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “ We’re just getting started .”

Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “ Facebook’s unjust enrichment .” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.

The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.

If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win.

The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court.

articles.title: Pediatric palliative care addresses the unique needs of seriously ill children and their families
articles.author:
<name>Khaliah Johnson, Associate Professor of Pediatrics, Emory University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/khaliah-johnson-2726772"/>
paras: Pediatric medicine generally entails caring for patients at the beginning of their lives – performing newborn checkups, treating childhood illnesses and supporting adolescents in their health as they move toward adulthood.
So people are often surprised to hear about specialists like us who work in pediatric palliative care , helping children facing serious illness who may be nearing the end of their lives.

This approach to care focuses on relieving suffering and addressing quality of life for children and families facing complex, life-limiting medical conditions. We also work to ensure that every family who needs it has access to this care, because right now, these programs aren’t available to most families globally who need them.
Pediatric palliative care is an approach that emerged out of the adult hospice and palliative care movement in the 1990s to early 2000s as a distinct discipline.

Globally, an estimated 7 million children die annually . Children with life-threatening health conditions often live longer between the time of diagnosis and death than adults. They benefit from approaches to care that consider the needs of their caregivers and family members .

Pediatric palliative care is provided by a team of professionals, including physicians, nurses, social workers, child life specialists, chaplains and other allied health professionals who take a comprehensive approach to a child’s care as they live with serious illness and ultimately approach the end of their life. The goal of this care is to support families in making every day as good as it possibly can be, regardless of whether or not a child’s life remaining is short. At the heart of this approach is the belief that each child has a right to holistic, empathetic care during illness and throughout end of their life that considers their unique social, cultural, physical and spiritual needs.

For example, an infant who is diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder that affects vital organ function and shortens life expectancy may need to be in and out of the hospital to manage acute illnesses and complex symptoms, such as pain and difficulty breathing. In turn, her parents may need help with deciding which treatments will be most helpful or may cause more suffering than benefit.

A palliative care team works with patients and caregivers to formulate a plan that ensures this baby gets care that affords her opportunities to experience as many happy moments as possible. This can improve the lived experience of this child and her parents.

Children and families who have benefited from pediatric palliative care describe these services as the supportive lifeline that helped them to navigate the complexities of diagnosis, life with serious illness and, ultimately, death and bereavement.

Over the past 20 years, there has been growing evidence suggesting the benefits of this approach. Children who receive care from pediatric palliative care specialists have less pain, nausea and other distressing symptoms that can affect their day-to-day function and overall quality of life.

Research also shows that children admitted to intensive care settings for managing life-threatening illness are more likely to receive care that aligns with their goals. When a palliative care specialist is consulted, patients are less likely to opt for life-sustaining therapies that would not change their long-term prognosis.

The U.S. is on the global forefront of pediatric palliative care: Nearly 80% of U.S. children’s hospitals have formal, interdisciplinary programs to provide this specialized care. But access to services in a clinic setting or at home is less consistent. Not every hospital-based palliative care program is connected to outpatient or home-based services, creating gaps for patients and families who need to access this supportive care between hospitalizations.

Generally, palliative care in the U.S. is more readily available in urban settings and at academic medical centers than in rural areas and community hospitals. These differences are most pronounced in rural states and the Southeast , a region of the country that has historically had health disparities across racial and socioeconomic differences . It can be difficult for children in these places to access patient-centered, interdisciplinary supportive services.

Outside the U.S., pediatric palliative care can be even more difficult to access. Though it’s hard to measure , estimates suggest that more than 21 million children worldwide would benefit from a pediatric palliative care approach.

More than half of the world’s population live in countries where the availability of any palliative care is defined as either emerging or progressing, according to the World Health Organization. Only 14% of countries – 28 total – are considered to have advanced levels of palliative care development. The numbers are fairly similar for pediatrics, with one study identifying only 11 countries as reaching the highest level of pediatric palliative care development.

As many as 97% of children in need of this approach live in low- and middle-income countries . Children in these countries have less access to medical diagnostic and therapeutic interventions and are often diagnosed at later stages of illness with less access to curative therapy.

The types of pediatric serious illnesses seen in the developing world are also very different from the landscape in the U.S. The greatest need for pediatric palliative care in developing nations – about 30% of cases – is in children with HIV . Among other children needing palliative care , about 18% are living with complications from prematurity, roughly 16% suffer from congenital malformations, and about 16% are dealing with injuries leading to severe neurologic impairment.

In contrast to many high-income settings, children with malignant diseases such as leukemias and solid tumors represent a relatively small proportion – about 4% – of patients who would benefit from a palliative care approach. In these regions, the predominant ailments are HIV/AIDS, premature birth and birth trauma, congenital anomalies and injuries.

In low- and middle-income countries, essential medications like morphine, used for controlling pain and other symptoms, often aren’t available . In addition, healthcare workers often haven’t been trained in foundational principles of palliative care .
On top of that, many of these countries don’t have the political infrastructure to provide basic healthcare , much less facilitate developing a comprehensive palliative care program for children.

The good news is that there are existing models for countries that are starting from scratch to build upon. And there’s room for innovation. Established community partnerships and technologies can be leveraged in new ways – for instance, using online learning and video conferencing to help train healthcare workers and build relationships.

We believe pediatric palliative care is the heart of what healthcare should be when a child faces a serious, life-limiting illness, regardless of where they live in the world. Because even when medicine cannot cure, it can always heal and comfort.

articles.title: Menopause can quietly weaken bones – here’s what research reveals about protecting them
articles.author:
<name>Priya Bhardwaj, Senior Researcher in Orthopedic Surgery, Washington University in St. Louis</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/priya-bhardwaj-2610112"/>
paras: A skeleton hanging on a door or standing in your neighbor’s yard for Halloween looks like a finished structure. But the skeleton inside a living body is constantly changing. Around menopause, those changes can tip toward bone loss, often without pain or another obvious warning.

I am a skeletal biology researcher at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. My work examines how hormonal and metabolic signals influence bone renewal. In my assessment, the quiet nature of bone loss makes menopause an important time to bring skeletal health into the conversation.

Bone loss can start accelerating before the final menstrual period. Natural menopause is confirmed only after 12 consecutive months without a period , when there is no other explanation. Bone loss can therefore accelerate before someone knows that their last period was their final one.

Bones are living tissues that continually renew themselves . During this process, called remodeling, cells known as osteoclasts remove old bone while other cells – osteoblasts – build its replacement. Estrogen helps regulate this renewal. As estrogen levels decline around menopause, removal can outpace replacement, contributing to bone loss and osteoporosis , a condition in which bones become more fragile and porous.
Osteoporosis can affect women and men. It becomes more common with age but can also occur in younger people. A person often has no noticeable symptoms until a fracture occurs.

The timing is revealing. An analysis of 862 participants in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation , a long-term U.S. study of women in midlife, tracked changes in bone density in relation to their final menstrual period. On average, loss at the lower spine and near the hip was fastest from about one year before that period through two years afterward. It then slowed rather than stopped.

These findings do not mean that everyone experiences the same amount of bone loss or develops osteoporosis. They show why the menopausal transition itself deserves attention, rather than treating bone loss as a concern only for older women.

To assess a person’s risk of breaking a bone, clinicians consider factors such as low body weight, smoking, excessive alcohol use and whether a patient’s parent experienced a hip fracture. A bone density scan measures bone mineral density and helps assess fracture risk. It provides useful information alongside medical history and other risk factors.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, an independent panel of experts in preventive care, recommends screening for osteoporosis in women age 65 and older. It also recommends screening younger postmenopausal women when their health history and other risk factors indicate a higher chance of a fracture. This does not mean every woman needs a scan as soon as her periods change.

These recommendations address routine screening. People who already have osteoporosis, have broken a bone after a minor fall or have a disease or take medicines that cause bone loss need evaluation tailored to their circumstances.

A U.K. trial illustrates how identifying people at high risk and recommending treatment can help . More than 12,000 women age 70 to 85 received either usual care or screening, followed by treatment recommendations for those at high risk. Over five years, women in the screening group were less likely to break a hip. However, when the researchers considered osteoporosis-related fractures across different parts of the body together, they did not find a statistically significant reduction. The findings support screening linked to treatment in older women, but do not tell us when screening should begin during the menopausal transition.

Bones respond to the forces placed on them. Weight-bearing activities such as walking and stair climbing make bones support the body’s weight. Resistance exercises using weights, bands or body weight create additional forces on bones as muscles pull against them. Balance training, such as tai chi and exercises that practice shifting weight from one foot to the other, can improve stability and help prevent falls. Activity for bone health therefore involves more than one kind of movement.

An Australian trial published in 2018 tested whether supervised heavy resistance exercises and impact movements could improve bone density and physical function in postmenopausal women with low bone mass. After eight months, participants in that program had better results than those following a less intensive home exercise program. The women were carefully screened, and the training was closely supervised.

These improvements are encouraging, but improved bone density is not the same outcome as fewer broken bones: The trial did not establish whether its program reduced fractures. People with osteoporosis, previous fractures or physical limitations may need guidance on appropriate movements and loads. Building muscle strength and balance can support mobility as well as bone health. Choosing suitable exercise depends on a person’s own circumstances.

Nutrition contributes in a different way. Calcium supplies mineral that helps give bones their strength , while vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium . Adequate protein also forms part of a balanced diet. Calcium-rich foods include dairy products, fortified alternatives, canned sardines or salmon with edible bones, and vegetables such as bok choy and broccoli.

Calcium or vitamin D supplements may help when a person’s intake is insufficient or they have a deficiency that needs treatment. They do not replace osteoporosis medicines when those are needed. Nutrition and treatment work together.

Systemic menopausal hormone therapy — treatment that delivers hormones throughout the body — can relieve bothersome hot flashes and night sweats and help prevent bone loss and fractures. Its benefits and risks depend on age, time since menopause, medical history and the treatment used.

For women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset who have no medical reasons to avoid it, the balance of benefits and risks from menopausal hormone therapy is generally favorable for treating troublesome symptoms and preventing bone loss. This does not mean hormone therapy is suitable for everyone. Patients and clinicians should discuss their symptoms, bone health and individual risks, and revisit the decision over time.

Other osteoporosis medicines can slow bone breakdown or stimulate bone formation. Clinicians also consider other medical conditions and medicines that can weaken bones , including hormonal disorders, digestive conditions and long-term glucocorticoid treatment. Menopause may be only part of the explanation.

One example is primary hyperparathyroidism , in which one or more parathyroid glands in the neck produce too much parathyroid hormone. This can raise blood calcium and weaken bones. Identifying it can change the care plan. It illustrates why investigating the cause of bone loss matters, rather than simply attributing it to aging.

Advice about scans and treatment assumes people can obtain them. Looking beyond individual choices shows how access to care can shape the options available. One example comes from a 2025 audit of 22 Asia-Pacific countries and regions . It documented substantial differences in access to osteoporosis care. Bone density scan waits ranged from the same day to nearly a year, and gaps in coverage for medicines limited the affordability of treatment. The regional audit concerns osteoporosis broadly, not only menopause.
In other words, making prevention possible requires both public awareness and health systems that make scans, follow-up care and treatment accessible and affordable.

Menopause offers an opportunity to ask about the skeleton while a person still feels well. The answer may involve a risk assessment, suitable activity, nutritional changes or medical treatment. A bone health conversation can begin long before a fracture starts it.

Priya Bhardwaj is employed by Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. She serves on the Endocrine Society’s Bone and Mineral Special Interest Group steering committee and ASBMR Women in Bone and Mineral SIG Commitee.
