paras: It’s getting harder and harder to figure out what to eat. A scroll through social media raises many questions. Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein? What about fiber? Do I need supplements? Should I be making all my bread at home? What foods were recalled this week?
These questions make trips to the grocery store and mealtime decisions more difficult. For centuries, some people have turned to their religious texts and traditions for answers.
In “ Born Again Bodies ,” religious studies scholar R. Marie Griffith traces how Protestant Christian ideas on faith and the body shaped the development of American diet and fitness culture.

Through my decade of ethnographic research on religious food movements, I have found that many Americans are still turning to religion as they decide what to eat. I analyzed four religious alternative food movements in my 2025 book, “ Free-Range Religion .” I argue there that these movements aren’t just changing what they eat; they are working to reshape the American food system from the ground up.

Two of the sites I studied were Jewish farms that were providing experiential education opportunities for the local Jewish community. It was part of their larger mission to reconnect Jews to the land and to the agrarian roots of Judaism. They often point out that the ancient Israelites were an agrarian people and that many Jewish laws, values and holidays were shaped by that context.

At the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center in Falls Village, Connecticut, I worked alongside young Jewish adults participating in a three-month program, the Adamah Farm Fellowship , as they planted, harvested and prepared produce for their weekly community supported agriculture program. The fellows begin their days with a morning prayer session and take time away from their work on the farm to celebrate Shabbat together. The fellows also attend classes where they learn about the biblical laws and ethical concepts related to agriculture, alongside scientific research on sustainable agriculture.

I conducted my fieldwork during a “shmita” year, a year of rest for the land . Just as the Hebrew Bible instructed Jews to work for six days and rest on Shabbat, the seventh day, they were also instructed to work their land for six years and then let it rest in the seventh year, the shmita year.

Farms took different approaches to the “shmita” year: The Adamah Farm Fellows kept their fields in production and started a community garden to mark their observance of the “shmita” year. At the Pearlstone center in Reisterstown, Maryland, the farmers replaced their usual rows of vegetables with cover crops that would enrich the soil during its year of rest. They also canceled their community supported agriculture program and focused their educational programs on the Jewish texts and traditions of “shmita” and the importance of rest for all beings.

Another group I studied were followers of the Hallelujah Diet, a plant-based diet rooted in the biblical story of the Garden of Eden. In “ The Hallelujah Diet ,” first published in 2006, the Rev. George Malkmus determined that the ideal food system was laid out in the first chapter of the Book of Genesis, where God instructs humans to eat plants, fruits and seeds . In the Garden of Eden, Adam and Eve would not have had access to cooked food, so the Hallelujah Diet also prioritizes the consumption of raw, uncooked vegan foods.

I attended a Hallelujah Diet health retreat in Lake Lure, North Carolina, in 2015 with nine followers of the Hallelujah Diet. This was a small subset of Hallelujah dieters. In the summer of 2013, I attended a talk by George Malkmus in Charlotte, North Carolina, along with hundreds of Hallelujah dieters.

Religion scholar Annie Blazer found that followers of the Hallelujah Diet tend to believe that it will cure their ailments and help them lead long and healthy lives. I found that the reality is a bit more complicated.

The retreat guests were adopting the diet in the hope that it would help them address medical issues, but they were not solely relying on the diet to heal them. The retreat guests were also seeing healthcare professionals and taking medications, recovering from or scheduling surgeries, and visiting physical therapists.

The fourth site I studied was Baldwin Beef , a family-owned cattle farm that produced 100% grass-fed beef in Yanceyville, North Carolina. The Baldwins are Christian and raise their cows in line with their understanding that, according to the Bible, cows are meant to live on pasture and eat grass.

This differs from the more common practice in the United States of moving cattle to feedlots for their final months and feeding them grain . The Baldwins also collaborated with a smaller-scale halal slaughterhouse to ensure that their cows experienced less stress in their final moments.

Christians and many other religious Americans have been wrestling with their relationship with animals and the ethics of eating meat since the 19th century. Many contemporary religious and nonreligious movements are reconsidering current animal welfare practices. In some cases, this means advocacy for vegetarianism or veganism and in others it means working to address issues in animal agriculture.

I use the term “free-range religion” in my book’s title for a reason: Americans belong to many communities at once, including religious communities, and the boundaries between communities are often porous.
For example, on the surface, the Hallelujah Diet book appears to be a Christian diet, written by a reverend. But I found that the reality was more complicated.

At the Hallelujah Diet health retreat I attended, all the participants were Christian – except for me, I’m Jewish – but the leaders of the retreat were Messianic Jews , who identify as Jews but believe Jesus was the Messiah. During our time at the retreat, we encountered a number of theological differences within our group, but our hosts encouraged us to remain focused on our shared interest in improving our bodily health.

In our educational sessions, medical doctors were cited as sources alongside biblical prophets, reflecting the range of authorities Hallelujah dieters recognize. The retreat participants similarly incorporated an array of practices into their daily lives, including yoga, meditation and the use of essential oils.
They saw some of these practices as part of their spiritual practice, while others were curtained off as “new age” and were seen as practices they engaged in outside of their Christianity.

As British anthropologist Mary Douglas demonstrated many decades ago in “ Purity and Danger ,” religion plays a central role in food choices as communities make determinations about what is considered clean and unclean. For many religious communities, food rules bring them together through shared values and identities but also separate them from others.

That is certainly happening today. Many communities still use food as a way to establish boundaries for membership. Jewish communities, for example, regularly establish rules around what people can bring to events to preserve the kosher status of synagogue kitchens. The kosher laws include restrictions on the types of meat that can be consumed and prohibits mixing meat and dairy in the same meal, so keeping a kitchen kosher requires communal adherence to these rules.

But these food decisions are also bringing religious and nonreligious people together in interesting ways and creating new collaborations in their efforts to transform the food system. The Jewish farmers from Adamah and Pearlstone are now part of a large umbrella organization, also called Adamah , that engages in interfaith climate advocacy work at national and international levels.

All of the groups I studied identified a concern regarding the food system. For the Jewish farmers, it was that Jews had become disconnected from food production. For the Hallelujah dieters, it was a concern that people were not eating the diet that they believed humans were created by God to eat in the Garden of Eden. For the Baldwin family, it was a concern that modern beef production did not align with biblical descriptions of cattle grazing on green pastures.

For these religious people, the solution was to start a farm or a diet that would provide a pathway for people to choose a different relationship with food or food production. These groups started small, with changes to their individual diets and commitments that shape their own approaches to producing food, but they all aspire to improving the entire food system.
Adrienne Krone serves on the board of the Center for Jewish Food Ethics

articles.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
articles.author:
<name>Jason Walker, Associate Professor of Psychology, Health and Wellness, Adler University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jason-walker-1372946"/>
paras: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades , according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo .

Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.
Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently.

Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.
More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations .

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services , according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice.
Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions.

Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.

Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.
We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K.
Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.
The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines.
Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.
Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.
Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities.
Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture.
Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts.

Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.
The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

articles.title: US wildfire damage is on pace to triple by mid-century, but there are affordable ways to lower the risk
articles.author:
<name>Virginia Iglesias, Earth Lab Director, University of Colorado Boulder</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/virginia-iglesias-2210786"/>
paras: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.S. is on pace to triple by mid-century , my colleagues and I found in a study just published.

The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire don’t have to be overly expensive .

The 2026 wildfire season began with historically low mountain snowpack , early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s hottest summer on record intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out.

Colorado’s Aspen Acres Fire destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving Knowles Fire overtook them near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in Spokane, Washington , damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate.

In Colorado, the summer monsoon season brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures.

Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had burned more than 318,000 acres by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also well above average . The U.S. spent 48 consecutive days at Preparedness Level 5 – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a 10-year average of 25 days annually.

Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a century of fire suppression has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned.

Rising temperatures caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying nearly doubled the area burned in western U.S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change.

More people also now live in and at the edges of wildland areas , raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round.
These interacting factors have helped nearly quadruple the annual area burned in the western United States since 2000.
They also contribute to the growing threat of fast-growing fires , which can overwhelm emergency response.

In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2.7% of fires analyzed but accounted for 78% of documented structures destroyed and 61% of reported firefighting costs.

A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster.
The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U.S., raising the risk of damage.

Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk expanded tenfold , increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building.

My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean up to 449,000 structures lost between 2026 and 2060.

We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations.

We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities . In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire.
These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now.

For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with Class A fire-resistant roofs and ember-resistant vents that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. Removing flammable debris , mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. Community programs are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk.

Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the Colorado fire code increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0.6% and 4.2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable.
Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it.

Beyond individual buildings, prescribed burning and appropriately designed forest-thinning operations can reduce fuels and alter fire behavior before flames reach neighborhoods. Utilities can strengthen infrastructure and reduce the probability of ignition while limiting disruptions from preventive power shut-offs. Insurance companies can reward measurable risk reduction and help sustain coverage in communities working to become safer.

These measures work best when they reinforce one another . The odds of losing a home to wildfire depend on its construction, its immediate surroundings and the broader neighborhood. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to wildfire risk. As the threat grows, strategies tailored to the environmental, social and economic realities of each community are more important than ever.
Virginia Iglesias receives funding from the National Science Foundation and from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety

articles.title: Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia , a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov , a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.
The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names , that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views , and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters .

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

articles.title: In Battle with Fire Department, Queen Anne Residents Win Parking Victory
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A quiet Queen Anne street has become a battleground between the Seattle Fire Department, residents wanting to park their cars, and the simple laws of geometry, but it looks to be Seattle's own parking regulations that have lost the battle – for now.

For decades, there's been an intermittent problem along the upper portion of 14th Avenue W, near Interbay along the west slope of Queen Anne Hill. The street is only around 15 feet wide, narrowing to as little as 14 feet and eight inches. With a row of on-street parking for residents, that isn't usually wide enough for a Seattle Fire Department ladder truck to easily pass through, depending on the exact width of the parked cars. Either the fire truck operator needs to inch their way down 14th to ensure no parked cars get hit, or they need to find another route.

Earlier this year, at the fire department's urging, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) announced that the street would be entering a new era, with on-street parking prohibited to improve Seattle Fire Department (SFD) response times.

"For every minute we are delayed getting to a fire, roughly that fire doubles in size, and so that increases the risk to you all," Seattle Fire Captain Tim Taylor, based out of Greenwood's Station 21, told Queen Anne residents at a community meeting held on the change this May. "When a rig can't get through or has to try to negotiate a very tight space, those are all things that are going to count directly against patient outcomes. That's the reality that we're dealing with."
Taylor noted that SFD had responded to these specific 14th Avenue blocks 73 times between the beginning of 2022 and this past March.

"We have six documented times where they took the time to send updates to the battalion chiefs and to leadership saying: 'Hey, we had a significant delay due to vehicles blocking and parking on this block,'" Taylor said. "I can tell you, I run into delays quite often. Just traffic or whatever, I don't often take the time to document it. It has to be pretty important for me to take the time to actually send the documentation that we were delayed on a response."

The idea of making parking adjustments to improve public safety might be expected to be non-controversial, but at the May community meeting, the pushback on the change was intense. Residents along 14th repeatedly pressed city staff on finding another path forward, with things turning so combative that one attendee had to be asked to leave after presenting an obscene hand gesture to city staff.
Though the discussion had been arranged to hear residents' concerns about the new parking restrictions, an expectation was laid out at the top: this adjustment was moving forward.
"I do find that it is very important to state at the beginning, this decision is not going to be changed," Rebecca Duran, executive aide to District 7 Councilmember Bob Kettle, told attendees.

And yet, just a few months later, SDOT announced that the decision had in fact been changed. A six-month pilot will evaluate whether vehicles can remain parked on the street "as long as they fit within the available right of way without interfering with reliable emergency vehicle access." A painted line has been added to the length of the street, with signs directing drivers to only park between the line and the curb.

"If your vehicle does not fit the marked area, you can’t park," SDOT's website on the change states. "Together with SFD, we’ll monitor how well the new design supports reliable emergency vehicles’ access. The results will help inform next steps."

On a recent visit to the street, The Urbanist found parked vehicles that were all within the constraints of the painted line on the street – even if that meant that a significant portion of their vehicle was up on the curb. That's also not allowed under the rules of the pilot, which state vehicles have to be 62 inches wide or less to be able to park on the street.
During that May meeting, residents pleaded with the SDOT planner present to essentially grant permission to park on the curb, but were rebuffed.

"The curbs are not actually designed to hold the weight of your vehicle, so you can end up damaging that and the underlaying structure if you park on the wall," SDOT Deputy Transportation Operations Director Matt Beaulieu said that night.

Getting questions answered about how this new parking scheme will be determined to be a success involved a lot of finger pointing within City departments. SDOT referred questions from The Urbanist to the Seattle Fire Department, which then noted that the Seattle Police Department is in charge of parking enforcement.

"Standard parking enforcement practices led by Seattle Police will be in effect. Seattle Fire has no role in enforcement," SFD spokesperson Kim Schmanke wrote. "Seattle Fire will evaluate delays to responses along the route due to access issues and if there were any reported obstructions noted during the non-emergency times."

SPD's parking enforcement division is not as well-resourced as other areas of the police department, with Mayor Katie Wilson recently proposing to eliminate several parking officer positions that had been sitting unfilled for several years. Most of the parking enforcement officer (PEO) resources are focused on areas of the city that have paid parking programs, or in responding to complaints as directed by other officers. With paid parking set to expand to Upper Queen Anne and Alaska Junction, that could mean even less resources for parking enforcement in other areas of the city.

With SFD evaluating response times and SPD maintaining control over enforcement, the pilot appears set up in a way that implicitly condones parking on the curb. But another precedent is potentially being set here, and that concerns SFD's requirements around fire lanes. With some exceptions, Seattle's current fire code requires access roads used by fire department vehicles to have an "unobstructed width" of not less than 20 feet.

But that standard is clearly not being met on 14th Avenue W, which if explicitly acknowledged within City bureaucracy could open the door to more flexible designs elsewhere, clearing a path for greater pedestrianization and traffic calming interventions. In the UK, a fire lane access road is generally only required to be around 12 feet.
"Seattle Fire agreed to this pilot knowing the constraints of the road width and SDOT’s capabilities," Schmanke wrote.

Depending on the way this pilot plays out, the results could have wide-ranging impacts beyond the sleepy confines of 14th Avenue W. For now, drivers will be able to park their cars, regardless of whether doing so involves going up on the curb.

articles.title: Seattle’s oldest Black church delivers ballots on Capitol Hill
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: First African Methodist Episcopal Church , the oldest Black church in Washington state, led a community march to the ballot box on Sunday, marching from the congregation’s 14th Ave home above Capitol Hill to the ballot box on Broadway.

Following services, participants walked half a mile through Capitol Hill to deposit their ballots at Seattle Central College , honoring previous generations while rallying civic engagement ahead of Tuesday’s Election Day.
“Because of their tears, their blood, and their sacrifice, we are now able to do this freely,” said Pastor Carey Anderson , urging younger voters to remember the legacy behind the ballot.
Marchers stressed the impact voting has on the city. “Whatever happens in your daily life is affected by the people who are in charge,” said participant Oveta Hunter .
Fellow marcher Kim Dudley framed participation as an ongoing family responsibility. “We can’t complain if we don’t vote,” she told CHS. “Get out here, take that chance, and vote.”

articles.title: A sour note on E Union: Building issues force closure of Central District’s Meter Music School
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Meter ukelele camp (Image: Meter Music School)

The Central District has lost a music school. After 15 years of guitar, singing, piano, banjo, drums, and ukulele lessons, Meter Music School has shuttered its E Union location as instruction continues at its Columbia City headquarters.
Director Brendan Bosworth confirmed the closure with CHS Monday as the school announced the shutdown to students current and past.

“Our building in the Central District needs major upgrades, so we made the decision to bring all of our programming over to our Columbia City location,” Bosworth said. “It was a wonderful 15 year run on East Union Street.”

Filings with the city show that an annual fire inspection in 2026 raised concerns regarding “unpermitted or non-compliant basement wiring” and structural issues related to unpermitted work on the 1900-era building the music school has called home.

In July, the Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections issued a notice of violation citing the years ago unpermitted conversion work and failure to secure a change of use permit to establish a music institution.

Meter began the pre-application process for working with the city to address the violations but the costs apparently didn’t pencil out for Bosworth or the property’s longtime owners, area real estate investors Charles Ragen and Wenjun Chen .
On Capitol Hill, structural problems and costs around a 96-year-old commercial building on 15th Ave E led to the exit of three businesses in September.

The Meter change will leave a hole in the string of businesses along E Union just west of 23rd and will mean a few changes for area families with young students who have attended in-person instruction at Meter.
In addition to independent instructors, other area options include the School of Rock chain’s studio in Montlake.
Bosworth says Gentle Giant Jiu Jitsu in Madrona has offered to take on the “MiniMeter baby & toddler classes” for area families. Meanwhile, the Columbia City Meter will now operate seven days a week.

articles.title: Sunday Video: How Does Philadelphia Even Exist
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Shortly after his visit to Seattle (where he attending a talk co-hosted by with The Urbanist), Ray Delahanty headed to the East Coast and did a similar event in Philadelphia. Ray had a lot to say about Philly's walkability and other positive aspects that often fly under the radar, sandwiched as the city is between New York City and Washington D.C., which have higher profiles nationally and internationally.

Delahanty declared Philadelphia might have the most walkable city core in the whole United States, which stems in large part from the thoughtful urban plan William Penn made for the city as he founded it in 1682, with plenty of narrow streets friendly to pedestrians.

"These streets are really a microcosm of what I'm thinking about when I think about walkability," Delahanty said. "It's not just about the physical act of walking. It's how a street handles motor vehicles. It's whether the streetscape is visually interesting. It's whether you feel secure. It's whether there are a ton of destinations nearby that are worth walking to."
Philadelphia – at least in the center city and South Philly neighborhoods that Ray explored – checked all those boxes. These distinctions puts it among North America's most walkable cities.

It's not all roses in the City of Brotherly Love. Philadelphia is also dealing with service cuts on SEPTA, a legacy metro system which has an impressive network of rapid transit lines across the region. As Delahanty highlighted, those cuts mean frequencies have decreased, especially on weekends, when even bedrock routes are now seeing mediocre 10-minute headways – not really in line with a top-tier transit city, which boasts a population of 1.5 million, amid a metropolitan region of 6.3 million. Hopefully SEPTA can get out of its downward spiral and back on the path of service improvements and growth.

articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Light rail ridership has been surging in the wake of the expansion of the 2 Line across Lake Washington on March 28 . The 1 Line now stretches from Federal Way to Lynnwood, with the 2 Line effectively doubling service from the Chinatown-International District to Lynnwood.

Four-minute peak frequencies in this overlapping segment are a major driver of ridership gains. Daily boardings remain above 160,000 even as the busy summer season has cooled. Gains in the Eastside portion of the light rail network have been less dramatic.

Due to construction defects and delays on the floating bridge portion of the 2 Line route, Sound Transit altered its plan and opened an Eastside-only "starter line" segment in 2024. That line extended to Downtown Redmond in spring 2025 and peaked just shy of 11,000 daily riders that summer, before fading over the fall and winter.

The extension of the 2 Line across the lake this spring has swelled ridership up to their summer 2025 peaks once more, but not significantly higher. The South Bellevue to Downtown Redmond segment averaged about 14,000 daily boardings in June, for example, but 11,330 in August after the World Cup ridership bump had subsided.

The 2 Line is almost assuredly garnering most of its ridership in its westside portion, from Seattle to Lynnwood. The caveat being we don't know for certain since Sound Transit told The Urbanist that it does not yet have the capability of separating 2 Line ridership from 1 Line ridership at the stations where both lines stop.

"Per our stats team, we do not currently have the ability to separate out 1 and 2 Line ridership in the core, but it is something the team is actively working on," Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said in an email. "We do not yet have a two 2 Line only whole system daily ridership number."

For the stations serving only the 2 Line, Sound Transit's ridership dashboard shows that Downtown Bellevue is leading the way, with South Bellevue in second. Downtown Bellevue averaged 2,541 daily boardings in August, while South Bellevue tallied 1,924, driven by its 1,500-stall parking garage.

Downtown Redmond is in third with just over 1,600 daily boardings, while Judkins Park (in Seattle) and Mercer Island fill out the top five. The 2 Line station struggling most for ridership is East Main, which managed just 480 daily riders in August.

Nearly every station west of Lake Washington is pulling in more ridership than even the busiest Eastside station. The exception is Rainier Beach, Kent Des Moines, and Star Lake, which are each below 2,500 daily boardings.
Westlake Station amassed 19,458 daily boardings in August, garnering more ridership than the entire East Link – the 12 stations served only by the 2 Line rather than both lines.

Eight of the top 10 stations for ridership are in Seattle. SeaTac's airport station (the second most-ridden) and Federal Way Downtown (in tenth) join the top 10 list. Seattle's top nine most-ridden stations all benefited from 2 Line expansion, which roughly doubled train frequencies, enticing more riders.

Since 1 Line and 2 Line ridership is currently lumped together in agency data (at least in overlapping stations) we don't know exactly how much of the load that the 2 Line is carrying at those stations.

The 1 Line is operating with a mix of four-car and three-car trains, while the 2 Line is typically two-car trains; so, the capacity of the 1 Line is greater. But riders traveling within the overlapping segment are likely to take whichever train comes first, which is effectively a coinflip when both are at eight-minute headways.

The lack of line-specific ridership data at Sound Transit could hinder the agency's ability to optimize its service patterns. However, a spokesperson did frame a solution to track the ridership by line, rather than in the aggregate only, as imminent.

The data shows a massive share of the agency's ridership passes through its top 10 busiest stations. The pattern has been fairly consistent in recent months, with about 65% of ridership happening in the top 10, versus just 35% in the remaining 16 stations in the corridor.

The largest ridership jump from August to September was at Shoreline South, which saw a 25% increase from just over 2,800 to just over 3,500 daily riders. This is likely the fall bus service change at work, and the increasing opportunity for bus-rail transfers after it – Route 522 now heads to Shoreline South instead of continuing along SR 522 to the University of Washington's Seattle campus, which means 522 riders headed to and from campus now hop a train in Shoreline. Another boost could be tied to the leasing up of new apartment buildings added near the station .
Federal Way was also a gainer in September, adding about 400 daily boardings and leapfrogging Roosevelt to become the ninth-busiest station for the month.

Meanwhile, the biggest ridership drops from August to September were at Stadium and Westlake. Stadium is yoked to the whims of sports fans and event schedules, and waning interest in the Seattle Mariners baseball team as their playoff odds evaporated must have hurt ridership totals. The drop of nearly 2,000 daily boardings at Westlake is more mysterious, but perhaps tied to a slowing of the tourism season. Sea-Tac Airport also saw a drop of roughly 1,000 daily boardings, in alignment with this hypothesis.

Overall, Sound Transit is largely sustaining ridership from its June peak during the height of World Cup fervor. In September, the 1 Line corridor came in just shy of 150,000 daily boardings, while the 2 Line hit nearly hitting 15,000 daily boardings in its exclusive segment.
Systemwide, September's ridership total is indeed down, but only moderately from the 178,264 daily boardings highwater mark in June.
What the trend will be in months ahead is an interesting question.

Sound Transit does not have any big light rail openings planned for nearly a decade, with West Seattle Link and Tacoma Dome Link extensions expected to come online in 2035, barring further delays. The Graham Street infill station could be a small boost around 2031.

And given the lack of housing development near the station, the recently inaugurated Pinehurst infill station isn't likely to move the needle much on systemwide ridership, at least in the near term. Starting in 2028, the rollout of Sound Transit's Stride bus rapid transit system could add a boost via bus-to-rail transfers, but impact will likely be modest.

Since Sound Transit torrid pace of light rail expansion is hitting a lull, light rail ridership growth will need to be organic – likely built on adding homes and jobs near existing stations and attracting more riders through consistent service quality.

Part of the decline from the June peak could be attributed to the agency's going from a month of nearly flawless execution to a period with several major service disruption and hiccups . Who can blame would-be riders for hopping on a bike or scooter or hailing a cab on days when significant disruptions occur?

The good news is that cities up and down the line are generally aiming to add housing near their stations – albeit to varying results . Sound Transit has also pledged improvements to maintenance and how it handles disruptions, hoping to lessen the sting and keep riders trusting light rail is a reliable way to get where they need go.
Even without major expansions in the near-term horizon, Sound Transit ridership appears to be trending in the upward direction all the same.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: Route 40 Upgrades Finally Reach Finish Line, Despite Business Opposition
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle and King County officials cut the ribbon on a suite of upgrades to Metro's workhorse Route 40 on Thursday – transit speed, reliability, and access improvements that have been in the works for the better part of a decade. The changes benefit around 9,000 daily transit riders traveling between Downtown Seattle, Fremont, Ballard, Crown Hill, and Northgate, but several key elements had faced significant opposition from business owners along the route.

Upgrades include three miles of business access and transit (BAT) lanes, targeted at some of the 40's biggest pinch points including stretches through the heart of Ballard, on either side of the Fremont Bridge, and along Westlake Avenue N. Sixteen bus stops were upgraded and more than 6,000 feet of new sidewalks were installed, with new crosswalks and curb ramps up and down the corridor.

"One of the busiest routes in King County – top five actually – has become faster, safer, and easier to use," King County Executive Girmay Zahilay said Thursday. "And for our riders, that means getting a little bit of time back and having a ride that they can count on. This is definitely worth celebrating and sharing gratitude with all of the teams who had so much to do with these improvements, as well as the community members who advocated for this."

Utility work that was able to happen at the same time as construction, including the replacement of 200 feet of water main, stretched out the implementation timeline, as did planning delays and budgetary turmoil. Backers of the 2015 Move Seattle Levy (which funded the project) had hoped to open the Route 40 upgrades as a RapidRide line in 2023, but ultimately scaled back the plan and abandoned the RapidRide branding in 2018 due to a budget crunch and worse federal transit funding outlook under the Trump administration 1.0.

Dedicated road space for buses is what drew the most organized opposition, which continued through the start of construction . In 2021, The Urbanist first reported pushback on the project's initial design coming from Eugene Wasserman, President of the North Seattle Industrial Association.

Wasserman has long been involved in the fight over completing the Missing Link of the Burke-Gilman Trail along Shilshole Way NW through Ballard and was one of the main opponents of the 2015 Levy to Move Seattle, which funded about 30% of the annual budget of the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). In opposing the Route 40 project, he cited potential impacts on routes used by freight trucks due to reallocating street space.

"It appears to the Maritime/Industrial community that SDOT is willing to sacrifice the viability of maritime/industrial businesses and their employees so that Amazon workers can get to their offices 5 minutes earlier," Wasserman wrote at the time. "Removing the number of traffic lanes the project does will have a substantial impact on our maritime/industrial businesses and will assist in the increasing gentrification of our industrial area."

While that opposition was initially confined to the freight community, it quickly expanded, with business groups in Fremont and Ballard also raising concerns. A 2023 letter signed by Pete Hanning, the head of the Fremont Chamber of Commerce and Mike Stewart, head of the Ballard Alliance, framed the project as out-of-date, citing a reduction in ridership on the Route 40 compared to pre-pandemic levels. Today, the Route 40 is one of the most popular routes in the Metro network, seeing only slightly less usage than the nearby D Line.

"SDOT did not conduct a thorough existing conditions study to identify the specific areas where improvements are needed, let alone the consequences that will result with respect to side-street congestion and overloaded vehicle queues, reliable movement of freight, and increased idling that will result in excessive carbon emissions," the 2023 letter stated.

Two separate traffic analysis studies were conducted on the changes, in response to the issues raised by project opponents and amplified by former Seattle City Council President Sara Nelson. Nelson came out against the bus lanes in 2023 and threatened to kill the transit project through the council budget process in 2024. In 2025, Nelson lost her reelection bid by 25 points to progressive nonprofit leader Dionne Foster.

Business opposition continued into 2025, as some design changes were made to respond to community concerns. SDOT relocated a bus stop location in Fremont and redesigned a new crosswalk at Westlake Avenue N and Halladay Street to reduce impacts on a nearby business. Most notably, the City of Seattle committed to piloting a new concept for the city, a freight-and-bus (FAB) lane along Westlake Avenue N to potentially mitigate some impacts to truck traffic.
Despite those changes, signs reading "Route 40 Plan: We Can Do Better" kept popping up along the route as the project was getting ready to start construction, as organized opposition continued.

Throughout its planning and construction, the project received significant support from multimodal transportation advocates, specifically Ballard Fremont Green Streets (BFG), previously known as Ballard-Fremont Greenways. An email campaign started by the group attempted to counter the opposition, a tactic that certainly helped the Route 40 upgrades to arrive at their ribbon cutting largely unscathed.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, who had been involved in the fight over upgrading the Route 40 as head of the Transit Rider's Union before being elected to lead the city, clearly took joy in being able to mark the occasion.

"These kinds of meaningful improvements matter as they make a difference in the everyday lives of residents of our city, and that is why I've also directed us SDOT to continue this trend to keep making our existing bus routes better at the same time as we launch new ones," Wilson said. "And so, really looking forward to continuing that work."

Zahilay told the crowd Thursday that initial data from Metro on the upgrades shows a 11% improvement in travel time for the Route 40 between Fremont and Ballard, which translates to 90 seconds saved on every bus trip, on average.

"Many of my neighbors and my friends rely on the 40 to work, to visit friends and family, to go to big events, to go shopping," Jason Weill, an advocate with Ballard Fremont Green Streets, said. "One BFG member told me that she commutes using the 40, and she used to deal with long delays, sitting through the bus [waiting] through multiple light cycles. But now the cars that used to block the lane have made way for busses."

But the improvements to the public realm extend beyond benefits to the bus riders themselves, with Lydia Heard of the Fremont Neighborhood Council noting that creating transit lanes has turned Fremont into a more walkable neighborhood.

"The reconfiguration of 35th at Fremont Place has a calming effect and transforms that corner into a more welcoming public space," Heard said. "But perhaps the biggest transformation is where the dedicated bus lane reduced [N] 36th to one general travel lane in each direction. This stretch of street, lined with popular businesses and often teeming with foot traffic, feels quieter and calmer most of the day. It is a much more enjoyable walking experience, and it is easier to cross the street. I think this is what we want for our community."

articles.title: Sound Transit Pilots Updated Pet Policy
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Sound Transit is piloting an updated pet policy on its buses and trains between now and Spring 2027. During the pilot, pet dogs will be permitted on board if they are leashed, well-behaved, and controlled by their handler. All other pets must remain in an enclosed carrier. As always, service animals are permitted in compliance with the ADA.

Prior to the pilot, dogs and other pets were only allowed on Sound Transit buses and trains in a carrier. In July 2025, the Sound Transit Board approved Motion No. M2025-34 , directing the agency to consider updating the rules to allow leashed dogs. This motion was motivated by the opening of Marymoor Village station as part of the Downtown Redmond Link Extension in May 2025. Marymoor Village station is next to Marymoor Park, a 640-arce park which includes a 40-arce off-leash dog area.

Will this pilot impact the passenger experience on Sound Transit? Probably not. In a presentation to the Executive Committee before the motion was approved, then-Acting Executive Director of Security & Fare Engagement Brian de Place acknowledged that passengers already take leashed dogs on Sound Transit buses and trains. While doing so did violate the rules, de Place noted “if the dog is leashed and generally under control, security will not engage with that passenger unless there is an actual disturbance”. In the year prior to this meeting, Sound Transit security only received 8 calls about pets.
There are few other notes pet owners should be aware of before bringing their leashed dogs onboard:
If you encounter an aggressive animal or other issues, call or text Sound Transit security: (206) 398-5268. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.title: How the Federal Way Link Extension Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: In December 2025, Sound Transit welcomed the first passengers aboard the Federal Way Link Extension. The three new stations on the 1 Line provide improved transit connectivity for many south King County residents. An accompanying bus service change in March 2026 improved frequency on many bus routes and adjusted a few bus routes to better connect with the new Link stations. While some routes lost ridership, many other routes welcomed new passengers. Link increased the total number of transit trips in south King County with nearly 10,000 combined weekday boardings at Federal Way, Star Lake, and Kent Des Moines stations.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in south King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.

Route 181 serves as the primary east-west route between Federal Way and Auburn. Federal Way Transit Center has long been a busy stop as it connects passengers with many other bus routes. The new Federal Way Link station caused a 46% increase in Route 181 boardings at that stop each day, from 293 to 430 passengers. Overall ridership on Route 181 increased by about 114 passengers and the ridership at other stops was not significantly impacted.

Route 183 is a coverage route between Federal Way and Kent, via the new Star Lake station. Prior to the Federal Way Link Extension, the route connected to freeway bus routes 177, 193, and 574 at I-5 & 272nd St. That connection generated about 4 boardings per day for Route 183. Now, 71 passengers board Route 183 each weekday at Star Lake station, a 1,675% increase. This is still just a fraction of the 1,600 weekday Link boardings at the station as many Link passengers use the station’s 1,100 space parking garage. Both of the route’s termini, Federal Way and Kent, have a slight decrease in ridership. This may be from some passengers switching to Link at Star Lake rather than to another bus in Federal Way or Kent.

The A Line now runs in the 1 Line’s shadow between Federal Way and Tukwila. Thanks to fast and frequent service along Pacific Hwy, it was the most productive Metro route in 2024 . Now that Link offers a faster trip north from Federal Way, this title may be in trouble. Stops across the A Line have reduced ridership from 2025. At Federal Way Transit Center, boardings on the A Line have dropped 19%. Likewise, the number of passengers boarding the A Line at Pacific Hwy & 240th St (near Kent Des Moines station) has been cut in half. Part of this severe drop in boardings is due to the new A Line stop that opened next to Kent Des Moines station. When factoring in boardings at that stop, there is still a 24% decrease in A Line boardings near Kent Des Moines station. A similar change occurred at International Blvd & 200th St, next to Angle Lake station. Many passengers who previously rode the A Line to the Link 1 Line’s southern terminus in 2025 are now opting to board Link at one of the new stations. Despite this drop in ridership, the A Line still provides critical local service along Pacific Hwy. As the area continues to develop, ridership on the A Line will rebound.

Route 165 connected Burien and Des Moines with Kent and Auburn via the newly opened Kent Des Moines Link station. Since the new station opened, boardings on Route 165 at the nearby stops (Pacific Hwy & KDM Rd, KDM Station, Pacific Hwy & 240th St) have increased 50% (109 daily passengers). This increase is offset by 70 fewer boardings at Kent Sounder Station, suggesting some passengers have switched from Sounder to Link. The route’s termini both have slightly reduced boarding counts as well, likely also due to the new station. For instance, someone traveling between Normandy Park and downtown Seattle may have switched from the 165 + H Line to 165 + 1 Line for their trip. In August 2026, Route 165 was replaced by routes 164 and 166.

The Federal Way Link Extension also impacted a few Sound Transit Express bus routes. As these routes are operated by Pierce Transit, we do not have detailed ridership data for them (yet). Instead, this analysis will use the overall route ridership comparing April 2025 to April 2026.

Ridership on Route 574 increased about 10% year-over-year. This is mostly from more people traveling between Lakewood or Tacoma and Link in Federal Way. Route 574 previously connected with Link at SeaTac, so the FWLE likely did not attract too many new passengers. The August 2026 service change truncated Route 574 at Federal Way in exchange for a much needed frequency boost, which should further increase ridership.

Routes 577 and 578 form the primary bus connection between downtown Seattle and Federal Way. Most times of the day, these routes are still faster than Link for that trip. As a result, ridership has not changed too dramatically. Boardings are down 10% on both routes. Routes 577 and 578 both saw a more significant drop in ridership immediately after the FWLE opening in December, but ridership has since rebounded. Whether the recent ridership increases are due to the routes’ lower travel time or due to the World Cup and other seasonal ridership changes is still up in the air.

The Federal Way Link Extension is already making its mark on travel patterns in south King County. Local routes connecting with Link are busier than last year. Meanwhile, ST Express routes and the RapidRide A Line lost some passengers to Link. The August 2026 service change further improved local connectivity in south King County that should make transit the best option for even more trips.

While this article only covered a few routes, detailed ridership data for most King County Metro routes is now updated at seattletransitridership.com . In addition, the impact of the Crosslake Connection on bus routes in east King County was discussed in a recent article .

articles.author: <name>Meg van Huygen</name>
paras: We’re not going to say people don’t come to Seattle for the food, but they definitely come for the views. The Cascades to the east, the Olympics to the west, Mount Rainier to the south, and water everywhere you look. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
